stem: A 25-year-old gentleman involved in a MVA crash as an unbelted driver. He presented to the ER with a blood pressure of 80/50 and heart rate of 70. He was unable to move his limbs below the level of elbow flexion bilaterally. He also lost sensation below the shoulder level including sphincters. What is the most important first line management?
srcNote: (Neurosurgery) Source note (Midterm 426 F Q72): The related recall keys "B. vasopressin with IV fluid".
expl: Cervical cord injury (C5–C6 level) with hypotension and relative bradycardia = neurogenic shock → IV fluids first, then vasopressors (noradrenaline, ± atropine); immobilize. Steroids aren't recommended.

why.A: Methylprednisolone isn't recommended (complications, no clear benefit).

stem: A 30 y/o male, presented to the emergency department after fall from a height, he complains of severe pain at the back. On examination his BP is 85/45 mmHg, pulse is 50/min, RR is 18/min. There is a tenderness over the thoracic spines. He is unable to move both of his lower limbs with absent sensations. The rest of examination was normal. Which of the following is the most likely cause of his shock?
srcNote: ( Trauma ) Source note (Midterm 432 F Q13): A related recall records PR: 120 bpm and an uncertain key, "Answer is: C?" (Neurogenic). This Q is probably wrong since In neurogenic shock there is also bradycardia not tachycardia as in this case. “Neurogenic shock… With patients typically presenting with hypotension, bradycardia and warm, dry peripheries.” -Davidson page 20
expl: Hypotension with bradycardia, thoracic spine tenderness and paraplegia → neurogenic shock.

stem: A 55 y/o male presented with progressive unsteady gait, and bilateral hand numbness. He noticed that he has difficulty with fine hand movement. Examination revealed difficulty in tandem gait, hypertonia, exaggerated reflexes, and positive Hoffman sign. Which of the following is the clinical diagnosis?
srcNote: Conflicting source key: one version of this same case uses a different diagnosis for option A. Other source key (Final 435 F Q12 (p. 144)): A. Cervical radiculopathy. Ans: A (Localization of lesion within CNs). The other retained versions key Cervical myelopathy.
expl: Cord compression in the neck gives upper-motor-neuron signs below the level: clumsy hands and loss of fine movement, unsteady (spastic) gait, hypertonia, brisk reflexes and a positive Hoffmann sign → cervical myelopathy.

why.B: A stroke is sudden and usually one-sided, not progressive and bilateral.
why.C: Cerebellar disease gives ataxia with hypotonia and normal/pendular reflexes — not hypertonia, hyperreflexia or Hoffmann.
why.D: Lumbar stenosis affects the cauda equina (lower motor neuron) — it can't cause hand numbness or upper-limb UMN signs.

stem: 71 years old man known prostatic is referred to the oncology by his general physician. He has had back pain for the past 3 week and now is complaining of difficulty walking. His bowel and bladder function is normal. On examination he has tenderness over his lower thoracic spine and impaired proprioception in his lower limb on neurological examination. He has a hard craggy prostate on rectal examination but normal anal tone. Which of the following investigation is the most likely to reveal the diagnosis?
srcNote: (Localization of lesion within CNS) Source note (Final 439 A Q4; Final 439 A Q29): Related versions describe neck pain with a history of breast cancer, or arm weakness with a posterior mediastinal mass. Both source keys are "A. Spinal MRI".
expl: Known prostate cancer + new back pain + difficulty walking with sensory signs = metastatic spinal cord compression until proven otherwise. The investigation of choice is MRI of the whole spine (metastases are often multilevel).

why.A: X-rays miss early metastases and can't show the cord.
why.B: LP doesn't image the cord and is not indicated.
why.D: CT shows bone but not the cord/epidural tumour as well as MRI; it is used only if MRI is contraindicated.

srcNote: (confirm by the doctor) Incomplete recall: the stem only states "loss of fine movement"; only three options are supplied.
expl: Incomplete recall. Loss of fine hand movement is a sign of a cord (myelopathic) lesion — the key chose "spinal level".

why.B: A sensory level describes sensory loss, not fine motor loss.
why.C: The umbilical level (T10) is a sensory landmark, unrelated to fine hand movement.

stem: What is the anatomical landmark that you can use to make sure that you won’t injure the spinal cord with the spinal needle during lumbar puncture?
srcNote: Source note (Final 432 F • first list • Q6 (p. 214)): The related source lists "D. posterior superior iliac crest" and states "Answer:D at the level of L4".
expl: The line joining the iliac crests (Tuffier's line) crosses L4 (L4/5 space); the cord ends at L1–L2 in adults, so a needle below this level avoids the cord.

stem: What is the part responsible for middle finger sensation in Brachial plexus?
srcNote: ( hand ) middle finger sensation innervated by median nerve
expl: Dermatomes of the hand: thumb = C6, middle finger = C7, little finger = C8.

why.A: C5 supplies the lateral arm (regimental badge area).
why.B: C6 supplies the lateral forearm and thumb.

stem: Patient presented with lower back pain, radiating to the gluteal area back of thigh and lateral foot, loss of sensation over the lateral aspect of the leg and foot as well as the posterior of thigh with loss of plantar flexion. What's the level involved?
srcNote: (Localization of lesion within CNs) Source note (Final 437 A Q19): The related root-level versions describe an absent ankle jerk and numbness of the small toes, and key "S1". This retained version provides disc-level options and keys "L5-S1".
expl: Pain to the buttock, posterior thigh and lateral foot, with lost plantar flexion (and ankle jerk) = S1 root, which is compressed by an L5–S1 disc.

why.B: An L4–L5 disc compresses L5: weak big-toe/foot dorsiflexion and numbness of the lateral leg/dorsum of the foot.
why.C: L2–L3 affects the anterior thigh and hip flexion.

stem: A 35 year old lady presented to the emergency department complaining of retention for one day. She gave a history of progressive pain involving the back of thighs for two months prior to this event. Physical examination revealed bilateral foot drop and loss of sensation over the lateral aspect of both feet. There was a decrease in anal tone and peripheral sensation. Which of the following conditions may explain this presentation?
expl: Urinary retention + bilateral leg pain and foot drop + lower-motor-neuron sensory loss in the feet + reduced anal tone = compression of the lumbosacral roots → cauda equina syndrome (a surgical emergency: urgent MRI and decompression).

why.A: GBS is an ascending symmetrical weakness with areflexia; sphincters are usually spared early and anal tone isn't selectively lost.
why.C: Cervical myelopathy causes upper-motor-neuron signs and affects the hands.
why.D: Proximal myopathy causes hip/shoulder weakness without sensory or sphincter loss.

stem: A 35 yo lady presented with LL numbness up to umbilicus for 6 months and developed walking difficulty recently, she has intact sphincter control, on examination she has decreased sensation to pinprick. on imaging it showed intradural extra medullary tumor. What is the most likely tumor she has?
srcNote: (Localization of lesion within CNs) Source note (Final 434 A Q34 (p. 164)): The clinical variant describes progressive spastic lower limb weakness, sensory loss below the nipple line, incontinence and a normal upper-limb examination. Its source key is "D. Thoracic meningioma."
expl: The commonest intradural extramedullary tumours are meningioma and schwannoma (nerve-sheath tumour); a middle-aged woman with slowly progressive thoracic cord compression fits meningioma.

stem: A young patient after a hyperextension injury to the neck presented with C5 and C6 roots injury. What is the sensory loss?

opts.t: lateral aspect of arm and forearm

srcNote: (localization of lesions within CNS) Incomplete option D: "medial ??" is reproduced as written in the source.
expl: C5 supplies the lateral arm and C6 the lateral forearm and thumb → loss over the lateral aspect of the arm and forearm.

why.A: The volar hand is mainly C6–C8 (median/ulnar).
why.B: The "superior deltoid" alone is only part of C5.

stem: A 35 y/o lady presented with LL numbness up to nipple for 6 months and developed walking difficulty recently, she has intact sphincter control, on examination she has decreased sensation to pinprick up to the nipple. What is the level of her lesion?
expl: The nipple line is the T4 dermatome, so sensory loss up to the nipple = T4 sensory level.

why.C: T8 is roughly the costal margin/xiphoid region.
why.D: "T8 neural loss" doesn't match the nipple level.

stem: A young boy came to you with neck pain, he had a history of trauma two weeks ago, what is the diagnosis?
expl: Keyed atlanto-axial subluxation: a child with neck pain after trauma (the film was in the source) — the C1–C2 joint is especially vulnerable in children (large head, lax ligaments).

why.B: Lordosis is a curvature, not a traumatic diagnosis.
why.C: The key chose subluxation over fracture for the shown image.
why.D: Spinal stenosis is a degenerative condition of adults.

stem: A 70-year-old lady presented with a 2-year history of bilateral lower limb numbness and inability to walk after walking for 15 minutes. Her symptoms were progressive, and she had to lean forward on a shopping cart while walking. Her clinical examination didn't reveal any neurological deficit. What is the likely clinical condition?
expl: Bilateral leg numbness after walking a set distance, relieved by leaning forward (shopping-cart sign — flexion widens the canal), with a normal neurological exam = neurogenic claudication from lumbar canal stenosis.

why.A: Vascular claudication is calf pain relieved by standing still, not by bending forward; pulses would be weak.
why.D: Diabetic neuropathy is constant "glove and stocking" numbness, not exertional.

stem: a 30-year-old gentleman presented with progressive neck pain and bilateral hand numbness for 2 weeks duration. He was a known drug addict. He had no history of trauma or fever. Normal neurologic examination. What is the next step in management?
expl: An IV drug user with progressive neck pain and new bilateral hand symptoms has a red flag for spinal infection (epidural abscess/discitis) even without fever → MRI of the cervical spine (best for soft tissue, cord and abscess). The recall put "Ans B" inside option D.

why.D: X-ray is normal early and can't show an abscess or the cord.

stem: Pt. presenting with inability to extend his big toe. On examination there was loss of sensation over the lateral aspect of the thigh and upper leg. What is the level of his lesion?
expl: Inability to extend the big toe (extensor hallucis longus) = L5 root, which is compressed by an L4–L5 disc. L5 sensation covers the lateral leg and dorsum of the foot.

why.A: L2–L3 affects the anterior thigh and hip flexion.
why.B: L3–L4 compresses L4: knee jerk and medial leg.
why.D: L5–S1 compresses S1: plantar flexion and the lateral foot.

stem: A patient came complaining of upper limb weakness and numbness for 2 months. He had weak shoulder abduction and numbness over the lateral arm and weakened biceps reflex. Which nerve root is likely affected?
expl: Shoulder abduction (deltoid), numbness over the lateral arm and the biceps reflex are all C5.

why.A: C4 supplies the cape (top of the shoulder) and the diaphragm.
why.C: C6 is elbow flexion/wrist extension, brachioradialis reflex, and the thumb.
why.D: C7 is the triceps and the middle finger.
